research_concepts: similarity of teammate initiation profile to the absent player
minutes, initiations and same-position minutes as competing predictors
methodological_questions: Does the top-1 hit rate of each predictor (closest profile, most minutes, most initiations, most same-position minutes) exceed what chance or a trivial baseline gives?
Do the four predictors differ in accuracy, and is profile similarity still informative after minutes and initiation volume are accounted for?
How should absence spells, primary types and gainers be defined without using the outcome, given 148 spells and 11 cases?
How do regression to the mean, mechanical floors and multiple comparisons affect a 'largest gainer' (maximum) outcome?
What placebo or null distribution is appropriate (for example, pseudo-absences with the same player present)?

historical_evidence.finding: Tested whether a similar-profile teammate separates absorption from cascade. Mean similarity was 0.863 for ABSORBED vs 0.848 for CASCADE, and Spearman(sim, -gap) was -0.19 (wrong-signed). The record gives Embiid 23-24 as a case that cascades despite a Reed similarity of 0.94. Recorded failure evidence: 'Similarity does not separate absorption from cascade; almost always findable.' The recorded failure mechanism is B_powered_null, the limitation is label/classification error, and sample and power are NOT_RECORDED.

Absence validation. Real absences moved the association structure (V1(a) 16/23 above null p95; V1(b) +0.142, CI [+0.103, +0.187]). The simulation's magnitude prediction failed (V2a Spearman +0.288, p=0.077, CI [-0.244, +0.667]; V2b +0.253, p=0.115). Limited by small sample.
Shaper presence did not expand non-focal play-type entropy (d_entropy_nonfocal=-0.0455, n_ts=80, no CI). The paper reads this as 'rebalancing not expanding'.
A within-game adaptation effect was limited by selection or regression to the mean. The retrieved excerpt says the no-signal baseline had the highest dPPP.

Holdout play-type rank validation. The record notes that part of the apparent top-3 lift reflects league-wide high-efficiency play types (CUT, PUTBACK, TRANSITION), and its failure mechanism is C_artifact. This is a reminder to compare against a trivial baseline.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using profile similarity to a teammate to predict whether an absence is absorbed or cascades
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as an adequately powered null (B_powered_null) with a wrong-signed correlation. Similarity is almost always high and findable, and the limitation is label/classification error.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Predicting the magnitude of redistribution under real absences with a leave-one-out simulation
failed_approaches.why: The V2 gates failed with wide confidence intervals, and the record cites small sample.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Detecting a change in play-type diversity when a shaper is present
failed_approaches.why: The effect was near zero, with no uncertainty reported.

evidence_establishes: In FAM:SF-CHT-052, similarity to the absent player did not distinguish absorption from cascade, and the correlation was wrong-signed. Similarity values are compressed at roughly 0.85-0.86.
Real absences do change the offensive association structure (FAM:SF20 V1), so there is something to redistribute.
Prior absence-level work in this project is limited by small samples (FAM:SF20).
evidence_does_not_establish: Nothing retrieved tests whether the closest-profile teammate (or the most-minutes, most-initiations or same-position-minutes teammate) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types. FAM:SF-CHT-052 is the closest analogue but tests a different outcome (absorb vs cascade).
The retrieved records do not give a top-1 hit rate or a chance baseline for any gainer-prediction rule.
FAM:SF-CHT-052 records no sample size or power, so its null cannot be tied to the present n=148 spells / 11 cases.
None of the retrieved records separates similarity from volume (minutes or initiations) as a driver of gain.
own_inferences: Because similarity is compressed (about 0.85) and nearly always findable, the closest-profile teammate is probably often also a high-minutes, high-initiation teammate. The four predictors are likely to be collinear and to coincide on many spells, so a hit by one does not show that similarity matters.

Prior wrong-signed similarity evidence suggests the closest-profile predictor will do no better than the minutes/initiations rules, and possibly no better than chance. I expect any hit-rate advantage to come from volume rather than profile.

Defining 'largest gainer' as a maximum over about 8-10 teammates is vulnerable to regression to the mean and to a mechanical floor. Teammates with the most volume have the most room to gain in absolute counts, and in rate terms low-volume teammates with noisy pre-absence rates can show large apparent gains.
If primary types are defined from the same games used to measure the gain, the label is partly outcome-derived.

If 11 cases is the effective number of independent absent players and 148 is the number of spells (non-independent within player), power is limited. With a chance rate of about 1/9, roughly 4 of 11 hits would be needed for one-sided p<0.05, so only large effects are detectable.
The question bundles four alternative predictors, so there is a multiplicity problem unless one is designated primary.
uncertainties: Unclear whether n=148 spells and 11 cases refer to the same sample or to different levels (spells vs distinct absent players or cases passing a filter).
Unclear how 'primary types' and 'gain' (absolute possessions, share or PPP) are defined, and what minimum spell length is used.
Unknown teammate pool size per spell, so the chance baseline is uncertain.
The reason for each absence (injury, rest, ejection) and the replacement lineup are unknown.
Whether the 2025-26 playoff data is complete at the analysis date is not established, and the data window spans possible drift across seasons.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have treated the question as a direct, plausible test. The recorded powered null with wrong-signed similarity in FAM:SF-CHT-052, plus small-sample limits in FAM:SF20, moved me toward lower expectations and a design with a designated primary predictor, a chance baseline, a volume-controlled comparison and cluster-aware inference. This is proceed_with_changes rather than a plain proceed, with predicted results leaning null or inconclusive.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 11 cases (148 spells nested within them) give limited power to detect a top-1 hit rate above a chance rate of about 1/9. Only large effects are detectable, and spells within a case are not independent.
Profile similarity is confounded with minutes, initiation volume and position. Separating similarity from volume requires within-spell comparison or a conditional (matched) approach.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests the exact claim. FAM:SF-CHT-052 is an adequately powered, wrong-signed null on whether profile similarity separates absorption from cascade, which bears on the similarity arm. FAM:SF20 shows absence-level work in this project is small-sample limited. The volume-based predictors have not been examined in retrieved work.

risks.text: 11 cases / 148 spells nested within players gives a wide interval on the hit rate. Treat spells as clustered within absent player and report the cluster-level effective n.

Similarity, minutes, initiations and same-position minutes are collinear. A hit by one predictor may simply reflect volume, role or lineup structure. Absence reason, opponent, and who else is absent also confound.

The 'largest gainer' is a maximum over noisy teammate deltas, so it is prone to regression to the mean. Pre-absence baselines should come from a separate window than the one used to define the profile.
Primary types and the closest-profile ranking must be fixed from pre-absence data only, not from games used to measure the gain.

High-volume teammates gain more in absolute counts, and a teammate with a zero baseline in a type has more room to rise. Use both absolute and share-of-opportunity gain, and report the volume baseline.
The chance hit rate depends on the teammate pool size per spell. Compute a spell-specific expected hit rate (1/k) and a random-pick null.
Four predictor definitions and several gain metrics invite forking paths. Designate one primary predictor and metric in advance.
Small possession counts per type per spell make gains noisy, so the argmax can be unstable. Estimate split-half reliability of the ranking.
The derived play-type labels in the graph database come from play-by-play heuristics, and similarity is almost always high (FAM:SF-CHT-052). Classification error may blur profile differences.
Play-type mix and rotation patterns may drift across 2022-23 to 2025-26 and between regular season and playoffs.

design.estimand: For each absence spell, whether the teammate with the highest pre-absence initiation-profile similarity (primary predictor) is the teammate with the largest gain in the absent player's primary play types. Estimate the top-1 hit rate of this predictor minus the spell-specific chance rate (mean of 1/k), and compare it to the hit rates of the three volume predictors (minutes, initiations, same-position minutes). Secondary: the hit rate of similarity conditional on volume, using spells where the similarity-top teammate is not the volume-top teammate.
design.unit: Absence spell, nested within absent player-season. Case = absent player (11 cases).
design.sample: All qualifying spells in the 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons and playoffs, using complete data as of the analysis date. Fix inclusion rules before looking at outcomes: a minimum absent-player pre-absence initiation volume, a minimum spell length and possession count, primary types as the absent player's top 2 types by pre-absence initiations from a window excluding the spell, and a minimum k teammates with a minimum number of pre-absence minutes. Report the final number of cases and spells and the chance baseline. If 11 cases is the effective independent count, treat the study as exploratory.
design.power: Fix a minimum detectable effect before analysis. With 11 independent cases and a chance rate of about 1/9, about 4 of 11 hits is needed for one-sided p<0.05, so only effects of about +0.25 over chance are detectable. With 148 spells, use a cluster bootstrap by absent player or a mixed-effects logistic model with a random intercept per player, and report the interval. If the interval for the primary contrast is wider than ±0.20, label the result inconclusive rather than null.
design.controls: Primary baselines: random pick (1/k) and the pick-by-minutes and pick-by-initiations rules. Condition on teammate volume and position. Use a split of pre-absence games to define profiles and a separate window for baseline rates to limit regression to the mean. Compare absolute and share-based gain definitions. Include absence reason and the number of other absent rotation players as covariates, and exclude spells with multiple starters out if sample allows. Pseudo-absence placebo: apply the same procedure to games in which the same player is present, to test whether 'largest gainer' is just a noisy argmax.
design.falsification: The hypothesis is rejected if the similarity predictor's hit rate does not exceed the chance rate, or exceeds it by no more than the volume predictors, with a cluster-level interval that excludes the minimum effect of interest. It is also not supported if the hit rate in pseudo-absence placebo games is comparable to that in real spells. Prior evidence (FAM:SF-CHT-052) predicts a null for similarity.
design.multiplicity: One primary predictor (profile similarity) and one primary gain metric (share-of-opportunity gain in the absent player's primary types) are designated before analysis. The three volume predictors and the absolute-gain metric are secondary and Holm-adjusted across the secondary set. All other analyses are exploratory and labelled as such.
design.decision_rule: Supported: the cluster-adjusted lower bound of (similarity hit rate - chance) is above 0, the hit rate exceeds the best volume predictor's, and the placebo shows no comparable hit rate. Rejected: the upper bound is below the pre-set minimum effect of interest. Otherwise report inconclusive. If the volume predictors explain the hits, conclude that volume rather than profile similarity drives the largest gainer.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files and the graph-database play-type possession records for 2022-23 through 2025-26 (regular season and playoffs), as available on 2026-11-01, with the 2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13 and playoffs from 2026-06-21. Freeze the data snapshot and the play-type derivation version before analysis.

research_concepts: primary play types of absent player
methodological_questions: Does the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile gain the most in the absent player's primary play types?
Do minutes, initiations or same-position minutes predict the largest gainer better than profile similarity?
How to define absence spells and primary types with small sample sizes (148 spells, 11 cases)?
How to handle regression to the mean, mechanical floor effects, and multiple comparisons when identifying the largest gainer?
What baseline or placebo is needed for gainer-prediction accuracy (top-1 hit rate vs chance)?
args.query: absent player primary play types, largest teammate gainer predicted by closest pre-absence initiation profile, minutes, initiations or same-position minutes

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["player absence", "offensive reorganization", "play-type redistribution", "initiator usage replacement", "teammate similarity to absent player", "primary play types of absent player", "largest gainer among teammates"], "methodological_questions": ["Does the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile gain the most in the absent player's primary play types?", "Do minutes, initiations or same-position minutes predict the largest gainer better than profile similarity?", "How to define absence spells and primary types with small sample sizes (148 spells, 11 cases)?", "How to handle regression to the mean, mechanical floor effects, and multiple comparisons when identifying the largest gainer?", "What baseline or placebo is needed for gainer-prediction accuracy (top-1 hit rate vs chance)?"], "query": "absent player primary play types, largest teammate gainer predicted by closest pre-absence initiation profile, minutes, initiations or same-position minutes"}}
